claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.label: Gaps between groups, even whole classes, are due to extinction of connecting forms
claims.statement: Extinction has defined and widened the intervals between groups; even the distinctness of whole classes, such as birds from other vertebrates, results from the loss of many ancient forms that once connected their early progenitors.

operationalizations.text: Quantify morphological disparity and nearest-neighbor morphospace gaps between extant vertebrate classes (e.g. Aves vs. Reptilia, Mammalia vs. Reptilia, Tetrapoda vs. fishes) before and after including extinct stem-group fossils (e.g. non-avian theropods, non-mammalian synapsids, stem tetrapods), testing whether fossils systematically bridge the inter-class morphospace intervals.

Use dated phylogenies and fossils to identify stem groups with intermediate character combinations and estimate whether lineage extinction enlarged morphological gaps between surviving crown groups. Discovery and temporal loss of intermediates, especially on the bird stem, supports the claim.

For vertebrate classes and other well-fossilized higher groups, test whether stem fossils occupy morphological positions between the living classes and whether denser sampling shrinks the gaps. The claim is confirmed if connecting series are present and stratigraphically early, as with the dinosaur-bird transition, and refuted if a densely sampled class boundary shows a persistent morphological break with no intermediate stem forms.

obstacles: Soft-tissue, physiological, and behavioral characters separating extant classes rarely fossilize, restricting the test to skeletal morphology.
The fossil record cannot reveal forms lost without preservation.
Morphological gaps depend on character choice and surviving sampling.
Soft-bodied and microscopic groups rarely preserve the intermediate anatomies the claim requires, so the test is strongest for skeletonized vertebrates.
A fossil can narrow a gap without showing that the missing forms were utterly destroyed rather than still unfound.
Last appearances are smeared backward by incomplete sampling, which can exaggerate how suddenly a connecting series seems to end.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.label: Branches equally related by descent can differ greatly in amount of modification
claims.statement: A natural arrangement of groups must be strictly genealogical, but branches that are equally closely related to a common progenitor may differ greatly in how much they have been modified, and these differing amounts of difference are what is expressed by ranking them as different genera, families or orders.

operationalizations.text: For sister clades in time-calibrated molecular phylogenies (which by definition share identical time since divergence from a common progenitor), test whether sister branches frequently differ substantially in accumulated morphological disparity, evolutionary rate, and assigned Linnaean rank.

For sister clades of equal genealogical depth, compare morphological or molecular disparity and assigned Linnaean ranks. Frequent large disparity and rank differences among equally related branches support the claim.

For sister clades, which are equally related to their common ancestor, compare phenotypic disparity or morphological branch length and the Linnaean ranks later assigned to each side. The claim is confirmed if equally close branches often differ several-fold in accumulated modification, and refuted if sister clades are consistently similar in amount of change.

obstacles: Post-cladistic taxonomy increasingly eliminates paraphyletic groups and equalizes sister-group ranks, so pre-cladistic or rank-asymmetric classifications must be examined to test the second part of the claim.
Amount of modification has multiple legitimate metrics.
Morphological matrices are taxonomically selective.
The requirement that a natural arrangement must be genealogical is a rule for classification, and datasets do not test the word 'must'.
Molecular branch lengths are abundant, while the amount of bodily modification Darwin meant is available only where morphological matrices exist.
Rank differences between sister clades partly record later taxonomic taste rather than a measured quantity of change.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms
claims.statement: As a general rule, the older a fossil form is, the more it differs from living forms.

operationalizations.text: Correlate the geological age of fossil taxa with their morphological distance (patristic or character-space distance) from extant species, and measure the proportion of extant genera and families present in progressively older geological periods.

Within clades having morphological matrices, calculate distance from each fossil to extant relatives and regress it on fossil age while controlling for phylogeny and missing characters. A generally positive age-distance relation supports the claim.

For fossil genera binned by age, measure taxonomic or morphological distance to the nearest living relatives and test whether that distance increases with age. No age trend, or ancient forms as similar to living ones as younger fossils are, would refute the general rule.

obstacles: So-called 'living fossils' (bradytelic lineages) exhibit low morphological divergence despite ancient origins, representing exceptions to the general rule.
Morphological matrices are curated for selected clades rather than all life.
Distance depends on character selection and extant survivor bias.
Taxonomic rank is a coarse stand-in for amount of difference.
Living-fossil exceptions are expected under a general rule and have to be scored as exceptions, which softens the test.
Character matrices cover a subset of clades.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: A species that has gone extinct never reappears
claims.statement: Once a species has disappeared from the earth, the identical form never reappears, because any replacement would inherit different characters from its different progenitors.

operationalizations.text: Evaluate putative re-appearances of extinct species in the fossil record and living biota using high-dimensional morphometrics and genomic phylogenies to determine whether apparent reappearances are Lazarus taxa (continuous survival without fossilization) or homeomorphic convergence rather than identical re-evolution.

Search dated occurrence records for species with a substantial global absence followed by later occurrences, then audit taxonomy and dating. A validated reappearance of the identical biological species would refute the claim; no such cases supports it only within detection limits.

Inspect species ranges for a disappearance followed by a later occurrence of the same species after a gap too long to be one continuous population. A later population that must be a new origin of the identical form would refute the claim; gaps explained by sampling would leave it standing.

obstacles: In the fossil record, taxonomy often defines temporally separated homeomorphs as distinct species a priori, creating circularity.
Distinguishing an unrecorded surviving lineage (Lazarus taxon) from extinction followed by iterative evolution requires dense stratigraphic and phylogenetic sampling.
Lazarus taxa usually reflect sampling gaps rather than true global extinction.
Morphospecies identity may not equal biological-species identity.
Incomplete sampling creates gaps that look like disappearance and return.
Identical form is unstable where fossils are feature-poor and species names are applied inconsistently.

claims.label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
claims.statement: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.

operationalizations.text: Test in paleontological time series whether geographic occupancy and site abundance systematically decline in the time bins preceding a taxon's last appearance, and in contemporary ecological time series whether population declines and range contractions precede local extinction as competing taxa increase.

In ecological and fossil time series, test whether increases of putatively favoured competitors predict declines of others and whether declining occupancy or abundance precedes last appearance. Consistent competitor-linked decline and pre-extinction rarity support the claim.

In fossil occurrences, test whether occupancy declines in the intervals before last appearance beyond a sampling model, and in modern assemblages test whether increases in one species are matched by decreases in others. Pre-extinction rarity and negative abundance coupling would confirm the two clauses; extinctions that are as often preceded by high abundance, once sampling bias is removed, would refute the geological clause.

obstacles: In the fossil record, sampling and preservation biases (the Signor-Lipps effect) can create an artificial pattern of apparent decline before extinction if not corrected with occupancy/sampling standardization.
Declines to rarity can be driven by abiotic environmental change rather than competitive displacement by favoured forms alone.
Sampling decline creates apparent rarity before last fossil occurrence.
Shared environmental forcing can produce reciprocal abundance trends without competition.
The Signor-Lipps effect makes taxa look rare before their true last occurrence.
Calling the increasing form the favoured one uses the outcome the explanation is meant to predict.
Ecological time series are short relative to extinction.

claims.label: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
claims.statement: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.

operationalizations.text: Compare survival, growth rate, and fecundity (fitness components) between inbred/selfed progeny and outcrossed progeny (across strains or varieties) across plant and animal species; significantly higher fitness in outcrossed progeny (heterosis) and lower fitness in inbred progeny (inbreeding depression) confirm the claim.

Meta-analyse controlled crosses at graded genetic distances for offspring survival, growth, fertility and reproductive output. Higher performance after moderate outcrossing and lower performance after close inbreeding support the claim; flat or opposite average effects refute it.

Compare vigour and fertility among offspring of crosses between varieties or strains and offspring of close inbred matings, using inbreeding coefficient as the predictor. Higher fitness of the crosses, and lower fitness as inbreeding increases, would confirm the contrast; no relationship, or a reversal after maternal effects are removed, would refute it.

obstacles: Crosses between very distantly related varieties or incipient species can occasionally exhibit outbreeding depression due to Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibilities or disruption of local adaptation.
Outbreeding depression can occur at large genetic distances.
Crossing experiments are unevenly distributed among taxa and traits.
Fitness of crosses versus close matings is published experiment by experiment rather than in one open database.
Maternal effects, purging, and heterosis specific to crops can inflate the apparent benefit of crossing.
Wild populations are less completely measured than livestock and cultivated plants.

claims.label: Reciprocal crosses between the same two species often differ greatly in success
claims.statement: The ease of crossing two species often differs greatly depending on which species is the father and which the mother, showing that crossing capacity depends on imperceptible differences confined to the reproductive system.

operationalizations.text: Quantify reproductive isolation asymmetry ($|RI_{A \times B} - RI_{B \times A}|$) in reciprocal interspecific crosses where both directions were tested in plants and animals, and test the prevalence and magnitude of significant directional asymmetry in seed set, fertilization, or F1 viability/fertility.

Compare fertilization, offspring number, and viability in both reciprocal directions for the same species pairs. Large repeatable direction effects support the claim; symmetry across well-powered pairs opposes it.

For species pairs crossed in both directions, compare offspring production with the sexes reversed. Frequent large asymmetries support the claim; consistently equal reciprocal success would refute the statement that the difference is often very wide.

obstacles: None of significance; reciprocal cross asymmetry is directly measured in standard diallel crossing designs.
Cross records are decentralized and taxonomically uneven.
Major compilations often average or sum reciprocal outcomes, erasing the contrast.
Direction-specific tables for plants, Fucus, and vertebrates are scattered.
A difference in success does not by itself locate the cause in an imperceptible reproductive detail.

claims.label: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties
claims.statement: The dominant species, those that range widely over the world, are most diffused in their own country and are most numerous in individuals, most often produce well-marked varieties.

operationalizations.text: Regress the number of recognized infraspecific taxa (subspecies and varieties) per species against geographic range size, regional occupancy, and local abundance across regional and global floras, controlling for taxonomic effort.

Model the number or probability of recognized infraspecific varieties as a function of range size, occupancy and abundance across regional floras, controlling sampling and taxonomy. Positive associations for all three dominance measures support the claim.

Regress the number of well-marked varieties per species on geographic range, local occupancy, and abundance, within regional floras, with sampling effort as a covariate. A positive partial association for wide, common species would support the pattern; no association after effort is controlled would refute it.

obstacles: Widespread and abundant species attract more taxonomic attention and herbarium collection, which can inflate the number of named varieties unless sampling effort (specimen count) is controlled for.
Sampling effort inflates both range and recorded varieties.
Abundance is poorly estimated by opportunistic occurrences.
Widespread species are collected and split more often, which manufactures varieties.
Abundance, range, and 'variety' rank are complete together only for some regional floras.
Darwin's dominance criteria (world range, local diffusion, and numbers) are only partly observed in the same records.

claims.label: Lung-bearing vertebrates descend from an ancestor with a swimbladder
claims.statement: All vertebrates with true lungs have descended from an ancient ancestor that had a swimbladder used for flotation, which natural selection converted into a lung.

operationalizations.text: Perform ancestral state reconstruction of gas-filled pharyngeal organs (paired ventral lungs vs. dorsal hydrostatic swimbladders) on a time-calibrated vertebrate phylogeny integrating developmental gene expression and fossil osteichthyan data; the claim is confirmed if a dorsal flotation swimbladder is reconstructed as ancestral to lungs, and refuted if paired respiratory lungs arose first and gave rise to swimbladders.

Combine vertebrate phylogenies with developmental, anatomical, and gene-expression characters for lungs and gas bladders, and reconstruct the ancestral organ and its function. Homology and an ancestral flotation bladder support the claim; independent origins or an ancestral lung refute its stated direction.

Code lung versus swim bladder, and flotation versus respiration, on a molecular vertebrate tree and reconstruct the ancestral state for lung-bearing vertebrates. The claim is supported if that ancestor is reconstructed as having a flotation swim bladder and lungs are derived from it; it is refuted if lungs (or a non-flotation air organ) are ancestral and swim bladders arise later inside ray-finned fishes.

obstacles: Soft-tissue gas bladders rarely fossilize directly, requiring reliance on extant phylogenetic bracketing (Polypterus, lungfishes, coelacanths, actinopterygians) and osteological correlates.
Deep ancestral-state direction can remain model-sensitive.
Functional use in the ancient ancestor is inferred indirectly.
The flotation function and soft anatomy of the deep ancestor are rarely fossilized.
Coding lung and swim bladder as alternative states can smuggle in a homology decision.
Selection as the converting agent is not recorded by character order alone.

claims.label: Difficulty of first cross and sterility of hybrids correspond only loosely
claims.statement: Species that are hard to cross generally produce very sterile hybrids, but the correspondence between the difficulty of a first cross and the sterility of the resulting hybrids is by no means strict.

operationalizations.text: Compute the correlation ($r$ or phylogenetic generalized least squares slope) and residual scatter between prezygotic/first-cross incompatibility (proportion of pollinations or matings failing to yield F1 zygotes/seeds) and intrinsic postzygotic F1 hybrid sterility (pollen/ovule or sperm/egg non-viability) across interspecific crosses in plants and animals.

For species pairs with both measurements, correlate first-cross success with fertility of their F1 offspring and quantify residual variation. A positive but far-from-perfect association supports the claim.

Correlate an index of how hard a first cross is to make with the sterility of the resulting hybrids, across species pairs. A positive but noisy association, with many pairs off the line, supports a loose correspondence; a tight relationship or no relationship would refute the stated pattern.

obstacles: Crosses that completely fail at the first-cross stage ($RI_{pre} = 1.0$) cannot be assayed for F1 hybrid sterility, truncating the upper end of the joint distribution.
Paired measurements are scattered.
Successful-cross ascertainment biases estimates of hybrid sterility.
The open numerical compilation is essentially Drosophila.
Ascertainment favors pairs that someone managed to cross.
Premating scores are an imperfect stand-in for Darwin's 'difficulty of making a first cross'.
